694.title: Magha Puja, deeper
694.hook: the verses taught that day: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind (Dhammapada 183–185)
694.howItsDone: On Magha Puja, Theravada Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia visit temples, keep precepts, listen to teachings and walk three times around a shrine at dusk carrying candles, incense and flowers; the Ovada Patimokkha verses are often chanted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Losar, the Tibetan new year, brooms and new prayer flags. Your line: a fresh year.

Sabbapapassa akaranam. On a full-moon night in Thailand, Laos or Cambodia, those Pali words may be chanted in a temple hall, the opening of a short verse. In year one you met the night it remembers: the commentaries tell of twelve hundred and fifty monks who came to the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha without being called, and of the Buddha giving them the whole teaching in three short verses. You also met the first verse. Today, all three, and what the Long Discourses add about who speaks them.
screen: `SABBAPAPASSA AKARANAM.` → `THE NIGHT, REMEMBERED.` → `NOW, ALL THREE VERSES.`

segments.voice: The three verses are known as the Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation, and the Dhammapada keeps them as verses 183 to 185. Here's the first, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Look at the middle phrase. The Pali word Müller renders as good is kusala, which other translators give as skillful or wholesome. So the second move is more than being nice: it's taking up, on purpose, what actually helps. The second verse, paraphrased, calls patience the highest austerity, and nirvana the highest thing of all. Someone who strikes or insults others, it adds, isn't a true renunciant, however they dress. Patience sits where a reader might expect fasting or hardship. The third verse is a short list: don't blame, don't strike, live restrained by the training, be moderate in food, sit and sleep in a quiet place, and give yourself to the higher mind. Like the first verse, it begins with harm and ends with the mind. Now the Long Discourses. In the Mahapadana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 14, the Buddha tells of Vipassi, a Buddha of an age long past, gathering his monks and reciting these same verses. So the teaching of all the Awakened is taken at its word: in that telling, this is what Buddhas say. Some teachers read the three moves as a ladder: restraint, then goodness, then a clear mind. Others read them as one movement. The verses set them side by side, short enough to chant in a breath, and the tradition hears in them the heart of it.

segments.voice: Follow the breath in and out, and let the water settle: that's the clear mind of the first verse. Then bring to mind one harm you could hold back from, a sharp word or a careless habit, and one good thing you could do, a call, a gift, a hand. Hold both simply, and come back to the breath.
Magha Puja. The full-moon day remembering the gathering of the twelve hundred and fifty, and the verses: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of it. Three moves, short enough for one breath. Until tomorrow.

695.title: Saga Dawa
695.hook: the Tibetan month of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply
695.tomorrow: Year two close: his own words
695.howItsDone: During Saga Dawa many Tibetan Buddhists walk pilgrim circuits such as the Lingkhor around Lhasa, give to beggars and monasteries, free animals, keep vegetarian, recite mantras and make offerings, especially on the full moon of Saga Dawa Duchen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Magha Puja and its three short verses. Your line: the heart of it.

The circuit around the old city of Lhasa is already full by sunrise. People walk it clockwise, spinning prayer wheels, murmuring mantras. Some stop every few steps to bow all the way to the ground. Along the route, people sit with open bowls, and pilgrims press small notes into bowl after bowl. It's not a single holy day, and it isn't only in Lhasa. It's a whole month. In Tibet, this is Saga Dawa.
screen: `A CIRCLE AROUND LHASA.` → `BOWLS ALONG THE ROUTE.` → `A WHOLE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Saga Dawa is the fourth month of the Tibetan calendar, usually around May or June. Dawa means month, or moon. Saga is the name of a star group, a lunar mansion the full moon sits near that month. So: the month of Saga. What makes it holy? In Tibetan tradition, the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing are all remembered in this month, with the big day on the full moon, called Saga Dawa Duchen, the great occasion. You may remember Vesak, where Theravada lands keep all three on one full moon. This is a Tibetan cousin of that idea, with its own dates and customs: in Tibet, the birth is often marked on a different day, earlier in the month. Then comes the part people talk about most. Tibetan teachers say that during Saga Dawa, the effect of any action, good or harmful, is multiplied many times over; on the full moon, some say, by a hundred thousand. Some teachers put the stress on attention: a month when every small act is said to count for more, so people make them on purpose. They walk the pilgrim circuits, around the Jokhang, around Lhasa, and some walk all the way around Mount Kailash. Some families give up meat for the month. Some buy animals destined for slaughter and set them free. And they give, especially to anyone with a bowl out on the pilgrim route. A note pressed into a bowl, an animal set free, a day without meat: in Saga Dawa, each small act is treated as large.

segments.voice: Let three people or causes come to mind, one at a time: someone near you who could use something, someone you pass every day and never really see, a cause you've meant to help and haven't. Hold each for a few breaths and ask quietly what you could give: time, money, food, attention, a letter. No need to decide everything; just let one gift become clear.

696.title: Year two close: his own words
696.hook: the truths, the path, the middle-length, the long, the short, the connected, the numbered
696.howItsDone: Many Buddhists study the discourses through chanting, reading groups and Dhamma talks, and in many monasteries and homes a favorite verse or sutta line is recited daily or kept close as a reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Saga Dawa, the Tibetan holy month. Your line: the holy month. Today is the last day of year two.

A year ago, year two opened with a promise: the Buddha's own words. Not stories about him. Not commentary. The discourses themselves, as the early collections keep them. Some days it was a single line. Some days it was a long walk through a long sutta. Today, from the lookout, one line from each stretch of the road.
screen: `A YEAR OF HIS OWN WORDS.` → `ONE LINE FROM EACH STRETCH.`

segments.voice: First, the four noble truths, from the first sermon at the Deer Park: there is suffering; it has a cause, which is craving; it can end; and there's a way. Then the eightfold path, factor by factor, six days each: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. The line to keep: the middle way, between chasing pleasure and punishing yourself. Then the Middle-Length Sayings, read in order, and from there the raft: a teaching is like a raft you build to cross a river. You don't carry it on your head once you're across. Then the Long Discourses, and the Buddha's advice in his last rains, when he was ill: be an island to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, with the teaching as your island. Then the short books: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka. From the Sutta Nipata, the discourse on loving-kindness: as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so keep a boundless heart toward every living being. Then the Connected and the Numbered Sayings, and from the Book of Threes: keep the pot upright, so what's poured in stays. Last, the festival year: full moons, ghosts fed, robes sewn in a day, and the passing between the sal trees. All things end. There's a Pali word for all of this: buddhavacana, the word of the Buddha. Schools of Buddhism draw the edges of that word differently. Theravada keeps the Pali canon; Mahayana schools also treasure sutras that year four will open, each in its own terms. This year stayed with the early discourses. Not the whole forest. A good handful.
screen: `THE TRUTHS AND THE PATH.` · `THE RAFT AND THE ISLAND.` · `THE MOTHER AND THE UPRIGHT POT.` · `BUDDHAVACANA, HIS WORD.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let one line arrive every few breaths: suffering has a cause, and an end; the middle way; the raft is for crossing; be an island to yourself; a boundless heart, like a mother's; keep the pot upright; all things end. Let each one land, then let it go. If one stays longer than the others, let it; that might be the line for year three.

697.title: A poet tells the life
697.hook: a poet retells the Buddha's life as a Sanskrit epic, and year three begins inside it
697.howItsDone: Buddhists come to the Buddha's life through many tellings, from the discourses and commentaries to later poems like the Buddhacarita, and in some communities these stories are read aloud, studied in classes or told at festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed year two: buddhavacana, the word of the Buddha. Your line: you've read his words. Year three starts now.

Same prince, same road, a new voice. In year one this path walked through the Buddha's life the plain way: a dream, a grove, four sights on a road, a ride out at midnight, short scenes mostly from the old discourses and the commentaries. Then came a whole year of his own words. Now the life comes back as a poem. Not a monk's report: a poet's, with long descriptions, speeches, gardens, gods leaning in from the sky, and a father who can't stop worrying. For the next stretch of days, i'll read it with you, one scene at a time.
screen: `THE SAME LIFE, A NEW VOICE.` → `NOT A REPORT. A POEM.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Buddhacarita: the life, or the acts, of the Buddha. Tradition names its poet Ashvaghosha, and calls him a monk who was also a master of Sanskrit verse. This path follows an English translation by E. B. Cowell. So what changes when a life becomes a poem? First, the pace. A discourse might give the prince's comfort in a sentence; the poem lingers, so you hear the music in the palace and smell the gardens. Second, people speak. The king argues, a friend makes his case for pleasure, a charioteer pleads, and the prince answers each of them in his own words. You hear the arguments he had to get past, not only the result. Third, the sky takes part. Gods arrange what the prince sees. Doors open on their own. Some readers take these as wonders that happened. Others read them as a poet's way of saying the whole world was turning toward this moment. The poem doesn't stop to settle it. And fourth, it's still the same story: the dream, the birth, the sage, the sights, the leaving. It doesn't invent a new Buddha. It slows the old one down so you can walk beside him. Not new facts: the same steps, taken slowly, one canto at a time.

segments.voice: The poem begins with a city, the old home of a sage named Kapila, a king of the Shakya clan named Shuddhodana, and his queen, Maya. Hold the three in mind, a city, a king, a queen, the way you'd hold the first page of a long book before anything has happened. No need to guess what comes next; just stay with the opening.
Buddhacarita. A Sanskrit poem that tells the Buddha's life, credited by tradition to the poet Ashvaghosha. Today's word.

698.title: The birth, in verse
698.hook: the queen's dream, the grove, the child who takes seven steps (Buddhacarita 1)
698.howItsDone: Some Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth at festivals such as Vesak, and in some East Asian temples images of the newborn standing with one hand raised are bathed with sweet tea or water to recall the streams from the sky.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Buddhacarita, the Buddha's life told by a poet. Your line: the life as a poem.

A queen lies asleep, and in her dream a white elephant enters her side. In time she asks to go out to a grove called Lumbini. The king agrees, she goes with her women, and there, in the grove, the child is born. Year one told these scenes quickly, almost like a list. The poet won't hurry. He stops at the moment of birth and reaches for the old stories of India to compare it with. And then he lets the newborn do something no newborn does.
screen: `A DREAM OF A WHITE ELEPHANT.` → `THE GROVE CALLED LUMBINI.` → `A NEWBORN WHO WALKS.`

segments.voice: First, the comparison. The child comes from his mother's side, and the poet lines this up with the births of heroes and kings in older Indian legend: one born from a thigh, one from a hand, one from the head. The point isn't anatomy. It's company: this birth belongs with the great births his listeners already knew. Second, the steps. As soon as he is born, the poem says, the child stands and takes seven steps, firm and steady. Then he speaks. In paraphrase, he says he is born for awakening and for the good of the world, and that this birth is his last. Third, the world answers. Streams of water fall from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him, and flowers come down on the grove. And fourth, the mother. It was Maya's wish that took everyone to Lumbini. Year two told that she died soon after the birth, and the poem will say so too, in the next canto. So these first steps are taken in a grove his mother chose, by a child she won't see grow. Seven steps is where the poem puts the start of the road. The leaving, the searching, the sitting: every later scene is more steps on it.
screen: `A BIRTH AMONG THE GREAT BIRTHS.` · `SEVEN STEPS, AND HE SPEAKS.` · `WATER FROM THE SKY, COOL AND WARM.` · `THE START OF THE ROAD.` · then, large: `SEVEN STEPS.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can, or let your hand do the walking on your knee, and take seven slow steps, counting each one: lift, feel it move, set it down. At seven, stop and feel your weight on the ground. Then sit, and let the seven steps settle.
The birth. In the poem: a dream, a grove, a child born from his mother's side, who stands, takes seven steps and speaks. Today's word.
Your line: seven steps. A newborn's first walk, and a last birth. See you tomorrow.

699.title: Asita's tears, in verse
699.hook: the sage weeps that he will not hear the child teach (Buddhacarita 1)
699.howItsDone: Asita's visit is told in other Buddhist texts besides this poem, and it appears in paintings and carvings of the Buddha's early life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the birth, in verse, a newborn who stands and walks. Your line: seven steps.

A palace celebrating a new baby, and a guest nobody sent for: an old holy man, Asita, who has seen signs and come on his own. The king receives him with honor and brings out the child. Asita looks for a long time. And his eyes fill, and the tears run down. In a room like that, a holy man weeping over a newborn seems to mean only one thing. Year one met Asita in a few lines. The poem gives the scene room, and lets both men speak: a frightened father, and an old man who has to explain his tears.
screen: `A HOLY MAN NOBODY SENT FOR.` → `HE LOOKS, AND WEEPS.` → `A FATHER AFRAID.`

segments.voice: First, the king's fear. King Shuddhodana sees the tears and trembles. Is my son's life short, he asks; is some harm coming to him? It is the question a parent asks. Second, Asita's answer. Not for the child, he says. The child is well, and more than well. He will leave the kingdom behind, wake up, and teach a way out of suffering for the world. In the poem's image, paraphrased here, the teaching will be like a boat that carries people across a great flood. Third, the turn. Then why weep? Because I am old, Asita says. My time is nearly over. This child will teach, and I won't be alive to hear it. The tears are for himself. He arrived at the right house, too early in the story. He doesn't resent the child or pretend not to care. He weeps honestly, and he blesses what he won't share. And fourth, the shadow. In front of the king, Asita has said the boy will leave the kingdom. A father who wanted an heir has just heard he may be raising a wanderer, and that sentence will sit in the palace for years. Some people know a version of Asita's grief: a grandparent who won't see the wedding, a founder who won't see the school finished. His answer is to love it anyway, from where he stands.
screen: `IS MY SON IN DANGER?` · `NOT FOR THE CHILD.` · `I WON'T LIVE TO HEAR HIM.` · `THE BOY WILL LEAVE THE KINGDOM.` · then, large: `BORN TOO EARLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a teacher you'll never meet: a writer long gone, a grandparent's grandparent whose sayings got passed down, or someone not yet born who will teach what you can't. Let that person sit in the room with you; you don't have to say anything. Just let there be gratitude, and a little of Asita's ache, side by side.
Asita's tears. An old sage weeps over the newborn, not from fear for the child, but because he won't live to hear him teach. Today's word.
Your line: born too early. An old man's tears, and a blessing. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

700.title: Life in the palace
700.hook: music, gardens, the king's fear that his son will leave (Buddhacarita 2)
700.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the palace years when speaking about comfort, attachment and family love, and the story appears in temple murals and in children's classes in Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asita's tears, an old sage weeping because he won't hear the child teach. Your line: born too early. And today is day seven hundred.

In the evenings, music drifts down from the upper rooms of the palace. Women play and sing. The rooms open onto gardens. Down below, the poem says, the whole land seems to flourish after the boy is born. Everything a young prince could want is brought upstairs to him. And the man who arranged all of it is afraid. It's the king. He keeps hearing an old sage's voice telling him his son will leave the kingdom. So he has decided what to do about it.
screen: `MUSIC FROM THE TOP FLOOR.` → `A KINGDOM DOING WELL.` → `A KING WHO IS AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Year one told the palace years from the prince's side, in his own later words: three palaces, one for each season, and a life of great comfort. The poem moves the camera. It shows the palace through his father. First, the plan. The poem says plainly why the king fills the prince's days with pleasure: he remembers what Asita foretold, and wants the boy so delighted with home that he never thinks of the forest. The music isn't only a gift. It's a strategy. Second, the details. The prince grows up in the upper rooms, among music and dancing, while out in the kingdom the king rules well and does good works, as if he could hold everything steady by being good enough. Third, the family. The king arranges a marriage, to Yashodhara, and in time a son is born, Rahula. The king is glad: a grandson is one more thread holding the prince to home. And fourth, the fear underneath. Nothing in the palace is cruel. Every gift is real, and every gift is also a wall. The king isn't a villain; he's a father trying to write his son's story for him. Some listeners will know that father. Some have been him. The poem doesn't mock him. It shows how hard he's holding on, and quietly suggests the holding won't be enough.
screen: `THE PALACE, SEEN THROUGH THE FATHER.` · `PLEASURE AS A PLAN.` · `A WIFE, A SON, ONE MORE THREAD.` · `EVERY GIFT IS ALSO A WALL.` · then, large: `A FATHER'S FEAR.`

segments.voice: Look gently around the life you have for one thing you've been protected from: a hard truth a parent kept from you when you were small, trouble your neighborhood keeps out of sight, a phone that shows you only what you already like. Don't judge whoever built the wall, and don't tear it down in your head; just see it, and notice whether it came from love, or fear, or both.
Life in the palace. Music, gardens, a marriage and a son, all arranged by a king who fears his son will leave. Today's word.
Your line: a father's fear. Tomorrow, something finally gets through the walls. That's day seven hundred.

fill his life with every pleasure so he never wants to leave.

chat.says: Why did the Buddha's father fill the palace with music and pleasure?

He wanted to train his son in the arts a king must know.
